To sum up, the Guidance is a legislative rule because it makes new

The court’s rationale for finding the State Department’s Guidance to be a 
legislative rule rather than an interpretive rule rests substantially on the 
categorical nature of the Guidance. This may look superficially similar to the 
way courts think about the difference between policy statements and 
legislative rules, i.e., policy statements cannot be rigid and binding. But the 
similarity rests on the happenstance that the preexisting legal text being 
interpreted in National Council (the State Department regulation invoking the 
“best interests of children”) was non-categorical, such that a purported 
interpretive rule introducing a categorical approach would tend to be 
legislative.

1. A Simpler Approach"^ Several commentators have proposed that the 
distinction between legislative rules and guidance (at least when it comes to 
pohcy statements) can be rendered simpler and more predictable if the 
reviewing court, instead of asking whether purported guidance is “really” a 
legislative rule and confronting difficult questions about ‘binding effect,” 
simply asks whether the rule was in fact promulgated via notice and comment 
and, if not, treats it as having no binding effect if the agency attempts to rely 
upon it:
* * * [l]f an agency says initially that a pohcy statement is not a 
binding rule and then later treats it as if it were a binding rule by 
refusing to engage in genuine reconsideration of its contents in a 
subsequent case, a court should invafidate the agency’s action in the 
individual particular case on the basis that the action lacks sufficient 
justification in the record. However, in my view the agency’s failure

5 State and the Council argue over whether, before the Guidance, State and the accrediting 
entity sometimes took adverse actions against adoption agencies over soft referrals. But either 
way. State does not argue that those specific adverse actions compelled the Guidance as a 
categorical rule or created a legal effect that the Guidance merely explained. Instead, State says 
those actions suggest that a pre-existing obligation already existed. But as explained above, under 
the best-interests-of-the-child standard, no such categorical obligation existed.
